prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought atomic timekeeping to the 1e-18 level of uncertainty and stability.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B018 alone, Katori and Ye. The round-1 exchange tested it from several sides and the core did not move. The achievement is one identifiable idea, trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels in the clock transition while Doppler and recoil effects are suppressed. Its result is a measured number, uncertainty and stability near 1e-18, reproduced and compared in several independent laboratories. No member disputed its originality, maturity or independent confirmation, and the chair's summary records the same. The many-atom lattice clock also introduced physics that single-ion clocks do not have: collisional and spin-exchange shifts, and a many-body-limited regime that Ye's group analysed. That is why I read it as a physical advance and not only as a refinement of technique. Attribution maps onto the two names without an arbitrary cut, Katori for the concept and first strontium demonstrations and Ye for taking the clock to record accuracy and coherence. I have now written the citation around the lattice clock itself, as Olsson and Kroll argued, which answers the chair's question about wording. I do not count the five first places as merit. I weigh the substantive reasons that members gave, and those hold.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously after round 1 is not the lineage point but the discovery-character point that Pearce and Danielsson put sharply: a gain of degree in a measurement we already knew how to make, set against a new observational window. I think that is a fair description of how a reader could see B018, and if the committee places a high premium on a new messenger it is a legitimate ground for ranking B007 first. A second reservation is that the lattice step sits on cooling (1997), combs (2005) and ion control (2012), and that the narrow citation leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups. A narrow citation reduces the overlap but does not remove the omissions. Third, the redefinition of the second is still pending, which some would treat as a reason to wait. I do not think it should decide timing, but I cannot show that it is irrelevant. Finally, the priority between the early lattice proposals and the first operating clocks is still from my own recollection and nobody in round 1 verified it.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B007 first and argues that lattice clocks are a gain of degree while IceCube opens a channel that did not exist. He resolves the attribution problem by crediting conception and construction of the detector, not later leadership of the analysis, and asks the committee not to rank B007 lower only because its credit requires a deliberate choice.
responses.response: His resolution of the credit is better than I allowed in round 1. Halzen for the concept and Karle for construction is a defensible reading, and I accept that the diffuse flux is secure and that the credit need not be arbitrary. I still do not move, for two reasons. First, a deliberate choice among hundreds of collaborators is exactly where a wrong or contested name would draw criticism, whereas for the lattice clock the concept and the decisive demonstrations trace to two people whom every member who ranked B018 named identically. Second, I do not accept that a clock is merely a gain of degree. Reaching 1e-18 in a many-atom lattice turns millimetre-scale gravitational redshift into a measurement and opens searches for ultralight dark matter and constant variation, which are new access to nature in the same sense, although narrower. I do accept that this is a judgement about weighting, not a fact, and I would not call a B007 prize a mistake. My answer to the chair's question is that discovery character counts, but here it does not outweigh a cleaner credit.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the lattice-clock step is separable from cooling, combs and ion clocks, that the citation should be specific to magic-wavelength trapping, and that it might include a sentence acknowledging the earlier work. He also asks what settles the Karle and Yoshida question for B007.
responses.response: I agree that the step is separable, and his argument that the magic-wavelength lattice allows large atom numbers with negligible light shift is the technical reason. I now think I was too tentative in round 1 about the lineage worry. Ion clocks reached comparable uncertainty by a different route, and the lattice idea is not contained in the comb or in cooling. On the sentence acknowledging earlier work, I would keep it out of the citation and treat it as background in the committee's publicly released scientific material, because a citation that names predecessors starts to read as precision timekeeping in general. I also share his point that priority has not been verified. Since all members, including him, describe the credits the same way, I treat it as a flagged uncertainty and not a barrier. His question on Yoshida for B007 is a reason I put that candidate second rather than first, since nobody has shown how the names are settled.

responses.point: Olsson would keep the citation narrow because widening it to the optical-clock lineage would drag in Hall, Hansch, ion clocks and Lemonde and dilute the attribution, and she argues that waiting for the redefinition of the second would tie a scientific prize to an administrative decision.
responses.response: We agree on both points and I have adopted her wording in the citation. I would add one qualification that she may not share: a narrow citation protects the attribution but it also commits the committee to the claim that the lattice clock is the identifiable step, so the supporting text must then explain why Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom and Hinkley are not named, instead of leaving it implicit. On timing I side with her. The measured uncertainty is the discovery, and the redefinition follows from it. I note that her own alternatives are B008 and B003, which I rank lower for credit reasons, and that her willingness to accept IceCube later is consistent with my own view that B007 is a strong prize for a later or a different year.

responses.point: Johansson replies that a theory-only prize for B032 is coherent because the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems, not the gate proposals, and that pairing Cirac and Zoller with Bloch and Greiner is impossible under the three-person limit without dropping a theorist.
responses.response: This answers my overlap question: pairing with Bloch and Greiner cannot be done within three names, and I agree that dropping one of Cirac and Zoller would be the less fair outcome. I also accept that 2012 concerned a different achievement, so I withdraw part of the claim I made in round 1 that the 2012 prize makes B032 unbalanced. What remains is a narrower point: demonstrations of gates by Blatt, Wineland, Monroe and others would stay unrecognised if only the proposal were honoured, and Zoller's appearance in both B032 and B015 means a prize on one still shapes the other. His ranking of B018 above most condensed-matter entries and his own concession that opening rank in his field may reflect habit are useful. I keep B032 as an alternative and would support it as a pure theory prize if the committee decided it wanted one.

responses.point: Mehlig says that magic-wavelength trapping builds on laser cooling and combs already recognised in 1997 and 2005, that the case for B018 rests on precision reached and its uses more than on a new physical concept, and that fluctuation theorems are the stronger conceptual discovery.
responses.response: The overlap is real, but I think it argues for a careful citation, not a lower rank. The new element, a lattice at a magic wavelength where the light shift cancels, is a concept about trapping, not about frequency measurement, and it is not something that cooling or the comb implied. I do not accept that the case rests only on precision. The many-atom regime added collisional and many-body physics to the clock. On B002 I agree that the physics is secure, but I share the attribution objections made by Danielsson, Kroll and Eriksson. Four credited names for three places, with Crooks as the awkward omission by Mehlig's own account, and uncertainty over which of three results carries the citation, make B002 harder to write than B018. I remain open to it in a later year if the committee can agree what the cited result is.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will weigh a new observational window (B007) above a measured precision advance (B018). That is a judgement of weighting that I cannot settle from the evidence, and a reasonable member could resolve it the other way.

The priority between the earliest lattice-clock proposals and the first operating strontium clocks, and the specific roles of Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley and others, which rests on recollection and was not verified by anyone in round 1.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay a prize. I think not, but I cannot exclude that other members will see it as relevant.
Whether B007 can be defended as a two-name or three-name credit, which is the factor most likely to change the ordering of my first choice and first alternative.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents collaborations with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, Reinhold Schuch, J. Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti and Paul Indelicato, and training in Ingvar Lindgren's Gothenburg group. None of these is a credited name for any shortlisted candidate, so I record no specific conflict requiring recusal, and the round-1 disclosure is unchanged. I work in the same broad atomic-physics community as B018, B032 and B015, and as a theorist I may be disposed to see the many-body analysis of lattice clocks as physics. I have tried to weigh that against the committee's arguments.
